The Age of the United States Government Measured 13 August 2026

The median American is 39. Almost no one who governs them is.

Every age on this page is plotted against one fixed scale, starting at 25 — the minimum age the Constitution sets for holding federal office. The dotted line is the country itself.

Constitutional minimum for federal office No maximum has ever existed

Congress

Article I

The 119th Congress arrived in January 2025 as the third-oldest since 1789. The figures below are not quoted from anywhere — they are computed in your browser from the published date of birth of every seated member, and they move as the Congress does. The House runs slightly younger; the Senate remains a generation above it. Both have aged faster than the country they represent.

      The Executive

      President, Vice President, department & agency heads

      This is the widest spread anywhere in government: a president of 80 and a press secretary of 28 work in the same building, 52 years apart. The department heads themselves bunch in the early fifties and thin out upward, which puts the cabinet as a whole a shade below the Senate and roughly level with the House.

          The Joint Chiefs

          Uniformed leadership · statutory 4-year terms

          The one corner of Washington with a built-in clock. Four-star officers reach the top after roughly 35 years of service and are pushed out by law and by mandatory retirement, so the entire body sits inside a narrow band in its late 50s and early 60s. General Dan Caine has chaired the Joint Chiefs since April 2025. Flag-officer birth dates are not consistently published, so these are close estimates, marked with dashed rings.

          Share of career money that came from PACs, by generation

          Across every member with a filing history, the Silent Generation has taken about — the PAC share that Millennials have. Earlier versions of this page tracked only the oldest and youngest members and put that figure near five times — the gap is real, but it was roughly half this size once the whole chamber is counted. Read the caveat below before using it: age is not the only thing separating these groups.

          What kind of money each generation takes

          The mix shifts along with the amount. Corporate PACs supply — of itemised committee money to members born before 1981 and — of it to Millennials. Labour runs the other way. The single Gen Z member takes almost none.

          Read this before you use the generation numbers

          This is now every seated member, not a selection. Earlier versions of this page tracked only the oldest and youngest members, which inflated the gap; that warning no longer applies. The figures below cover both chambers in full. A census removes the sampling problem — it does not remove the three below, and a complete dataset invites more trust than the reasoning behind it can always carry.

          Career totals cover unequal spans. A member first elected in 1975 has forty years of receipts behind their percentage; one elected in 2024 has a single cycle. These are shares of very different amounts of money raised under very different rules, averaged into one number per generation.

          Age and era are tangled together. Older members started raising money when PAC cheques were the only practical way to fund a campaign. Small-dollar online fundraising only became viable around 2004 and dominant after 2018. First-cycle year correlates with PAC share at r = — on its own, so some of what looks generational is really just the year someone started.

          Seniority attracts PAC money regardless of age. Committee chairs and leadership raise more from organised interests because they hold the gavel, not because of when they were born. Every long-serving member on this page is also a senior one.

          How this was built

          Every number on this page is computed, not quoted. Ages, medians, averages and counts are all derived in your browser from each person's published date of birth, so the plots, the finder and the chamber figures recalculate every time the page loads and stay correct as the page ages. Earlier versions carried published chamber medians as static text; they no longer do.

          Congress is a census. The rest is not. Both chambers are complete — every seated senator and representative, with birth dates from the congress-legislators dataset, which is public, maintained, and carries a bioguide identifier and a birthday for every member. All nine Supreme Court justices, the Joint Chiefs and the serving cabinet are complete too. The governors are a selection covering both ends of the age range, and are labelled as such wherever they are counted.

          The six delegates from the District of Columbia and the territories sit in the House and raise federal money, so they appear in the finder and in the money analysis. They hold no floor vote, so they are excluded from the House median, which describes the 435 apportioned seats.

          Estimates are marked. Dashed rings and a “≈” mean the birth date is not reliably published — chiefly the uniformed service chiefs, and a small number of executive officials. Any average that includes an estimate says so.

          Term status is current as of 13 August 2026: eleven Senate retirements, two primary defeats, sixty House retirements and fifteen term-limited governors. Candidate ages come from published birth dates; a nominee is not a winner, so the ledger shows the range a seat can land in, not a prediction.

          One gap worth naming. When a member's next election is derived — House seats every two years, Senate seats by class — it is exact. Whether they intend to run again is not published in any machine-readable form, so retirement announcements are entered by hand and only a handful are recorded here. A badge reading “On the ballot” therefore means the seat is up, not that the incumbent is seeking it. The turnover section below, which does track the announced departures, is the reliable place to read who is leaving.

          Campaign finance is rebuilt from the FEC's own bulk downloads — candidate summaries for every cycle since 1980, itemised committee cheques since 2018. No API key, no intermediary. The trend charts use election cycles only and start at 1990, because senators raise almost nothing between races and the FEC's PAC field is incomplete before then. The current cycle is partial. Dark money, bundling and all state-level fundraising are invisible to this data. A high PAC share says who paid for a campaign; it is not evidence of a vote traded.

          The national baseline is a median age of 39.1 for the United States, per the Census Bureau.

          What is covered, and what is not

          Some parts of this page are a census and some are a selection, and a number means something different depending on which. Rather than describe that in prose that goes stale, the table states it — counted from the data itself every time the page loads.
